```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
set.seed(2026)
# non-ASCII characters in output and plots under a "C" locale
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "C.UTF-8"))
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(100 * x, d), "%")
```

In the post on [random experiments](../random-experiments/index.qmd) we saw that a single coin flip is unpredictable, yet over many flips a remarkable stability appears. Today we turn that observation into a number: the **probability** of an event. We will look at the classical definition, a trap that catches even experienced people, and the rules we use to compute probabilities.

## Statistical regularity

We repeat a random experiment $n$ times and count how many times $N_n(A)$ the event $A$ occurred. The **relative frequency** of $A$ is

$$f_n(A) = \frac{N_n(A)}{n}.$$

In the simulator below, choose an event and watch its relative frequency evolve in five independent runs.

::: {.ix-panel}
::: {.ix-title}
Relative frequency simulator
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
experiments13 = ({
  "Heads on a coin flip": {p: 1/2, draw: () => Math.random() < 0.5},
  "A six on a die roll": {p: 1/6, draw: () => Math.floor(6 * Math.random()) === 5},
  "A sum of 7 with two dice": {p: 1/6, draw: () => Math.ceil(6 * Math.random()) + Math.ceil(6 * Math.random()) === 7}
})
viewof exp13 = Inputs.radio(Object.keys(experiments13), {label: "Event", value: "A six on a die roll"})
viewof n13 = Inputs.select([100, 1000, 10000, 100000], {label: "Repetitions", value: 10000, format: x => x.toLocaleString("en-GB")})
viewof run13 = Inputs.button("New simulation")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sim13 = {
  run13;
  const e = experiments13[exp13], n = n13, paths = [], finals = [];
  // Keep log-spaced points so the chart stays light
  const keep = new Set([...Array(400).keys()].map(i => Math.round(Math.exp(i / 399 * Math.log(n)))));
  for (let k = 1; k <= 5; k++) {
    let hits = 0;
    for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
      if (e.draw()) hits++;
      if (keep.has(i)) paths.push({n: i, f: hits / i, run: `Run ${k}`});
    }
    finals.push(hits / n);
  }
  return {p: e.p, paths, finals};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const fmtP = x => x.toLocaleString("en-GB", {minimumFractionDigits: 4, maximumFractionDigits: 4});
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    height: 300, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {type: "log", label: "Repetitions n →"},
    y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "↑ Relative frequency", grid: true},
    color: {legend: false},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([sim13.p], {stroke: "#c62828", strokeDasharray: "5,4"}),
      Plot.line(sim13.paths, {x: "n", y: "f", stroke: "run", strokeWidth: 1.4}),
      Plot.text([sim13.p], {x: n13, y: d => d, text: () => "probability", dy: -9, textAnchor: "end", fill: "#c62828"})
    ]
  });
  return html`<div>${chart}<div class="ix-note">Final relative frequencies after ${n13.toLocaleString("en-GB")} repetitions:
    <b>${sim13.finals.map(fmtP).join(" · ")}</b>. The red line is the probability ${fmtP(sim13.p)}.</div></div>`;
}
```
:::

Whichever event you pick, the five paths start out chaotic and end up at the same value. This **statistical regularity** is the empirical basis of probability: the probability of $A$ is the number around which the relative frequency of $A$ settles.

This is the **frequentist interpretation**, and it is very useful for understanding what a probability means. As a definition, though, it has a serious problem: we cannot run infinitely many repetitions, so we cannot *compute* a probability from it. We need a way to find the red line without rolling a single die.

## The classical definition

When the sample space $\Omega$ is finite and **all outcomes are equally likely**, the probability of an event $A$ is

$$P(A) = \frac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{possible outcomes}} = \frac{N(A)}{N(\Omega)}.$$

For example, the probability that a card drawn from a 52-card deck is red is $26/52 = 0.5$. The definition immediately gives $0 \le P(A) \le 1$, $P(\Omega) = 1$ and $P(\varnothing) = 0$.

### The equally-likely trap

The condition "equally likely" is not a technicality. Roll two dice and record the sum, so $\Omega = \{2, 3, \ldots, 12\}$ with 11 elements. Is the probability of a sum of 7 equal to $1/11$? No, because the 11 sums are **not** equally likely. A sum of 2 arises only from (1, 1), while 7 arises from six pairs. The equally likely outcomes are the 36 ordered pairs:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sums
#| fig-cap: "Probability of each sum of two dice. The dashed line is the incorrect value 1/11."
#| fig-height: 3.6
omega <- expand.grid(d1 = 1:6, d2 = 1:6)
p_sum <- table(omega$d1 + omega$d2) / nrow(omega)

barplot(p_sum, col = "#9ecae1", border = NA, ylim = c(0, 0.18),
        xlab = "Sum", ylab = "Probability")
abline(h = 1/11, lty = 2, col = "#c62828")
```

The correct answer is $P(\text{sum } 7) = 6/36 = 1/6$, which is exactly where the simulator converges for the third event. The general rule: **choose the sample space so that its outcomes are equally likely**, and then count.

### Two examples by enumeration in R

When the sample space is small, R does the counting for us. What is the probability that two dice show **consecutive** numbers?

```{r}
#| label: consecutive
consecutive <- abs(omega$d1 - omega$d2) == 1
sum(consecutive)
mean(consecutive)
```

There are `r sum(consecutive)` favourable pairs, so the probability is $10/36 \approx$ `r fmt(mean(consecutive), 3)`.

A slightly more interesting one: the coefficients of $x^2 + k x + l = 0$ come from two die rolls. What is the probability that the equation has **rational roots**? This happens exactly when the discriminant $\Delta = k^2 - 4l$ is a perfect square ($0, 1, 4, 9, \ldots$).

```{r}
#| label: rational-roots
k <- omega$d1; l <- omega$d2
D <- k^2 - 4 * l
rational <- D >= 0 & sqrt(pmax(D, 0)) == round(sqrt(pmax(D, 0)))
omega[rational, ]
mean(rational)
```

We find `r sum(rational)` favourable equations, so $P = 7/36 \approx$ `r fmt(mean(rational), 3)`.

## Basic rules

Counting elements of sets under the classical definition gives the rules below. In the [next post](../kolmogorov-axioms/index.qmd) we will see that they hold for **every** probability, not just the classical one.

| Rule | Formula |
|---|---|
| Disjoint events | $A \cap B = \varnothing \;\Rightarrow\; P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ |
| Complement | $P(A') = 1 - P(A)$ |
| Union | $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ |
| Monotonicity | $A \subseteq B \;\Rightarrow\; P(A) \le P(B)$ |
| Difference | $P(A - B) = P(A) - P(A \cap B)$ |
| Symmetric difference | $P(A \,\Delta\, B) = P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A \cap B)$ |

The union rule extends to three events as the **inclusion–exclusion principle**, which we met for counts in the post on [events](../sample-spaces-events/index.qmd):

$$\begin{aligned}
P(A \cup B \cup C) = {} & P(A) + P(B) + P(C) \\
 & - P(A \cap B) - P(A \cap C) - P(B \cap C) + P(A \cap B \cap C).
\end{aligned}$$

In the calculator below you enter $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A \cap B)$ and see the probability of every region of the Venn diagram and of the usual events. The default values solve this problem: 60% of a town's pupils have a mobile phone ($A$), 40% have a computer ($B$) and 25% have both.

::: {.ix-panel}
::: {.ix-title}
Probability calculator for two events
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pv13 = Inputs.form({
  a:  Inputs.range([0, 1], {label: "P(A)", step: 0.01, value: 0.6}),
  b:  Inputs.range([0, 1], {label: "P(B)", step: 0.01, value: 0.4}),
  ab: Inputs.range([0, 1], {label: "P(A ∩ B)", step: 0.01, value: 0.25})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const {a, b, ab} = pv13;
  const r = x => Math.round(x * 100) / 100;
  const f = x => r(x).toLocaleString("en-GB", {minimumFractionDigits: 2, maximumFractionDigits: 2});
  const lo = r(Math.max(0, a + b - 1)), hi = r(Math.min(a, b));
  if (r(ab) < lo || r(ab) > hi) {
    const why = r(ab) > hi
      ? `An intersection cannot be larger than either event: P(A ∩ B) ≤ min{P(A), P(B)} = ${f(hi)}.`
      : `A union cannot exceed 1, so P(A ∩ B) ≥ P(A) + P(B) − 1 = ${f(lo)}.`;
    return html`<div class="ix-warn">Impossible combination. ${why}</div>
      <div class="ix-note">For these values of P(A) and P(B), P(A ∩ B) must lie in [${f(lo)}, ${f(hi)}].</div>`;
  }
  const onlyA = a - ab, onlyB = b - ab, none = 1 - a - b + ab;
  const rows = [
    ["A ∪ B", "at least one", a + b - ab],
    ["A Δ B", "exactly one", a + b - 2 * ab],
    ["A − B", "A only", onlyA],
    ["A′ ∩ B′", "neither", none],
    ["(A ∩ B)′", "at most one", 1 - ab]
  ];
  const svg = `<svg viewBox="0 0 320 200" style="width:100%;max-width:320px">
    <rect x="2" y="2" width="316" height="196" fill="#fff" stroke="#333"/>
    <circle cx="125" cy="100" r="68" fill="#4e79a7" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="#4e79a7" stroke-width="2"/>
    <circle cx="195" cy="100" r="68" fill="#f28e2b" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="#f28e2b" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="14" y="22" font-size="14">Ω</text>
    <text x="62" y="40" font-size="14" fill="#4e79a7" font-weight="600">A</text>
    <text x="252" y="40" font-size="14" fill="#d9771f" font-weight="600">B</text>
    <g font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">
      <text x="98" y="105">${f(onlyA)}</text><text x="160" y="105">${f(ab)}</text>
      <text x="222" y="105">${f(onlyB)}</text><text x="285" y="185">${f(none)}</text>
    </g></svg>`;
  const box = html`<div class="ix-row"><div></div><div></div></div>`;
  box.children[0].innerHTML = svg;
  box.children[1].innerHTML = `<table class="ix-tbl"><tr><th>Event</th><th>Meaning</th><th>Probability</th></tr>
    ${rows.map(([s, m, p]) => `<tr><td>${s}</td><td>${m}</td><td><b>${f(p)}</b></td></tr>`).join("")}</table>
    <div class="ix-note">Allowed values of P(A ∩ B) for these P(A), P(B): [${f(lo)}, ${f(hi)}].</div>`;
  return box;
}
```
:::

The calculator "complains" when the values are impossible. Try $P(A) = 0.8$ and $P(B) = 0.4$: $P(A \cap B)$ cannot drop below $0.2$, because then $P(A \cup B)$ would exceed 1, nor rise above $0.4$, because the intersection lies inside $B$. In general:

$$\max\{0,\; P(A) + P(B) - 1\} \;\le\; P(A \cap B) \;\le\; \min\{P(A),\, P(B)\}.$$

The rules are also easy to check by enumeration. For two dice, with $A$ = {sum is 7} and $B$ = {at least one six}:

```{r}
#| label: union-rule
A <- omega$d1 + omega$d2 == 7
B <- omega$d1 == 6 | omega$d2 == 6
c(`P(A ∪ B)` = mean(A | B),
  `P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)` = mean(A) + mean(B) - mean(A & B))
```

## Key takeaways

- The **relative frequency** of an event settles down over many repetitions; the value it settles at is its probability.
- The **classical definition** $P(A) = N(A)/N(\Omega)$ applies only when outcomes are **equally likely**.
- The rules for complements, unions, differences and inclusion–exclusion are the basic computational tools.
- $P(A \cap B)$ cannot take just any value: it is constrained by $P(A)$ and $P(B)$.

## Review questions

**1. Quick quiz.** Pick an answer and you will see right away whether it is correct.

::: {.ix-panel}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz13 = [
  {q: "Two coins are tossed and we record the number of heads: Ω = {0, 1, 2}. What is P(exactly 1 head)?",
   opts: ["1/3", "1/2", "1/4", "2/3"], ans: 1,
   why: "0, 1, 2 are not equally likely. The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT, and exactly one head occurs in HT and TH: 2/4 = 1/2."},
  {q: "If P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2, what is the probability that neither A nor B occurs?",
   opts: ["0.1", "0.3", "0.5", "0.7"], ans: 1,
   why: "P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B) = 1 − (0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2) = 0.3."},
  {q: "If P(A) = 0.7 and P(B) = 0.6, which value is impossible for P(A ∩ B)?",
   opts: ["0.25", "0.3", "0.45", "0.6"], ans: 0,
   why: "We need P(A ∩ B) ≥ 0.7 + 0.6 − 1 = 0.3. A value of 0.25 would give P(A ∪ B) = 1.05 > 1."},
  {q: "What is the probability that three births include at least one boy (boys and girls equally likely)?",
   opts: ["1/2", "3/4", "7/8", "1/3"], ans: 2,
   why: "Complement: P(no boys) = P(GGG) = 1/8, so P(at least one boy) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8."}
]
{
  const root = html`<div></div>`, score = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`, done = new Map();
  quiz13.forEach((item, k) => {
    const fb = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`;
    const btns = item.opts.map(o => html`<button>${o}</button>`);
    const opts = html`<div style="margin:4px 0 0 6px">${btns.map((b, j) => {
      b.onclick = () => {
        const ok = j === item.ans; done.set(k, ok);
        btns.forEach(x => x.className = "");
        b.className = ok ? "ix-picked-ok" : "ix-picked-no";
        fb.innerHTML = (ok ? `<span class="ix-ok">✓ Correct.</span> ` : `<span class="ix-no">✗ Not quite.</span> `) + item.why;
        score.innerHTML = `<b>Correct: ${[...done.values()].filter(x => x).length} of ${quiz13.length}</b>`;
      };
      return b;
    })}</div>`;
    root.append(html`<div style="margin:12px 0"><div>${k + 1}. ${item.q}</div>${opts}${fb}</div>`);
  });
  root.append(score);
  return root;
}
```
:::

**2.** If $P(A)/P(A') = 3/4$, find $P(A)$.

**3.** A loaded die satisfies $P(1) = P(3) = P(5)$ $= 2P(2) = 4P(4) = 2P(6)$. What is the probability of an even number?

**4.** Show that if $P(A) = 0.8$ and $P(B) = 0.4$, then $0.2 \le P(A \cap B) \le 0.4$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

2. $P(A) = \frac{3}{4}(1 - P(A))$, so $\frac{7}{4}P(A) = \frac{3}{4}$ and $P(A) = 3/7$.
3. If $P(1) = x$, then $P(2) = P(6) = x/2$ and $P(4) = x/4$. From $3x + x/2 + x/4 + x/2 = 1$ we get $x = 4/17$, so $P(\text{even}) = x/2 + x/4 + x/2 = 5/17$. This die does not have equally likely outcomes, yet the rules still apply.
4. The intersection lies inside $B$, so $P(A \cap B) \le 0.4$. Also $P(A \cup B) = 1.2 - P(A \cap B) \le 1$, so $P(A \cap B) \ge 0.2$.
:::
